# Novel fixture expected outcomes (hand-labeled, not part of the docs glob)

Counts are indicative, not graded (owner ruling 2026-08-14): a richer graph is acceptable
when every extra requirement is independently testable and every extra entity has
statements directly about it. The graded parts are the traps, the derived data (edges,
state machines, instances, flow views), and what the diagrams show.

The medium is a novel bible. Requirements are narrative obligations on the manuscript
and its parts; entities are characters, settings, the family, and the manuscript's own
structure. Nothing here is software and no entity is a system.

## Core entities (must exist)

| entity | stereotype | parent | attributes the prose gives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Manuscript | manuscript (or deliverable) | none | none |
| Chapter | chapter | Manuscript | none required (`title` acceptable) |
| Scene | scene | Chapter | `point of view`, `setting`, `goal`, `outcome` (typed, no value) |
| Ines Marlow | character (`actor` acceptable) | Marlow family | `age: 31`, `occupation: bookseller`; alias `Nessa` |
| Theo Brandt | character | none | `age` (see trap 2), `occupation: marine surveyor` |
| Callum Pryce | character | none | `age: 33`, `occupation: project lead` (at Pryce Maritime) |
| Dot Feeney | character | none | `age: 58`, `occupation: ferry office manager` |
| Marlow family | family | none | none |
| Port Alder | town (setting) | none | `population` acceptable, not required |
| The Lantern Room | bookshop (setting) | Port Alder | none required |
| Marlow House | house (setting) | Port Alder | none required |
| The notebook scene | scene (instance) | none required | `point of view: Ines`, `setting: the upstairs room of the Lantern Room`, `goal`, `outcome` (valued) |
| Harbor ledger | prop (or ledger) | none | none |
| Harbor wall | structure (setting detail) | Port Alder acceptable | none |

Stereotype labels are judgment and are not graded beyond being sensible for the medium.
Labeling the four characters `actor` is acceptable and makes the use-case and sequence
views draw them as actors; `character` is the expected judgment, and the flow clustering
then keys on the first listed entity, so every plot and arc requirement lists the acting
character first.

Borderline (acceptable, not required): Pryce Maritime, harbor council, ferry office,
the ferry, the Marlow lease, Theo's field notebook, the harbor crew, the takings ledger,
the eight chapters as individual entities under Manuscript (`Chapter 1: Arrival` ...).

Must NOT exist: `Nessa` (trap 1); the chapter file names and the `manuscript/`
directory (trap 6); `Sunday`, `close third person`, `past tense`, word counts, years,
the lantern (requirement detail on the Lantern Room); a `System` or `Novel` container
invented to hold everything (Manuscript is the deliverable and the only whole the docs
state above the chapters).

## Requirements

At least 60 statements across the six documents. Every one of the 23 plot scene lines is
its own requirement quoting its own list item; every one of the 9 arc transitions is its
own requirement (8 table rows plus the midpoint sentence). The scene lines carry a
`behavior` facet; the plan failure in chapter 5 carries `failure-mode`; the chapter
length bound carries `constraint` (or `quality` with measure `2,000 to 3,500 words`).

## Edges (the prose states these; types as listed)

- Manuscript → Chapter `composition` (cardinality `1..*` or `8`); Chapter → Scene
  `composition` `1..*`.
- Marlow family → Ines Marlow `composition` (Ines's `parent` follows it).
- Port Alder → The Lantern Room `composition`; Port Alder → Marlow House `composition`.
- Marlow family → The Lantern Room `association` or `dependency` (holds the lease).
- The notebook scene → Scene `instantiation`.
- Who knows whom (characters.md): Ines and Callum `association`; Dot and Ines
  `association`; Callum → Theo `dependency` (hires); Dot and Theo `association`.
- Plot scenes with two characters carry an edge from the actor to the other: Dot →
  Ines (tells Nessa), Ines → Dot (asks for the ledger), Ines → Theo (confronts; asks
  him to stay), Theo → Ines (refuses the report; offers the crack finding), Callum →
  Theo (leave out the crack), Callum → Ines (asks Nessa to drop the petition).
  `dependency` or `association`; the direction is the graded part.

Every edge above comes from a requirement; no arrow appears without a statement.

## Transitions and state machines

Two machines, one per lead, subjects `ent:ines-marlow` and `ent:theo-brandt`. States
(both): `stranger`, `acquaintance`, `rival`, `ally`, `beloved`. Initial (both):
`stranger`.

`sm:ines-marlow`, four transitions:
- stranger → acquaintance, trigger `Theo takes the upstairs room`
- acquaintance → rival, `Dot tells Ines who Theo works for`
- rival → ally, `Theo offers Ines the crack finding`
- ally → beloved, `Theo shores up the wall through the storm`

`sm:theo-brandt`, five transitions:
- stranger → acquaintance, `Theo finds the crack beneath the Lantern Room`
- acquaintance → rival, `Ines confronts Theo about the survey` (the table)
- acquaintance → ally, `Ines confronts Theo about the survey` (the midpoint paragraph)
- rival → ally, `Ines's plan fails at the council`
- ally → beloved, `Ines asks Theo to stay`

Checks: exactly one `nondeterministic-transition` (warning) on Theo's two
`acquaintance` transitions (trap 3). `dead-end-state` (info) on `beloved` for both
machines: the docs say beloved is where the book leaves them, so this is the
acknowledged final state, not a gap. No `unreachable-state`. `unhandled-event` (info)
fires with many (state, trigger) pairs and is not graded. The premise in README.md names
no stance, so nothing adds states such as `lovers` to either machine.

## Instances and conformance

One instance: the notebook scene (plot.md "A worked scene"), `instantiation` to Scene.
Its four attribute names (`point of view`, `setting`, `goal`, `outcome`) all exist on
Scene, so the mechanical check files no `nonconformant-instance`, and `conform-instance`
finds the values sensible (the point of view is a character, the setting is a place from
settings.md). Default `view:object/scene` with the notebook scene as its one member. The
worked scene is not merged into Scene and does not become a second Scene type.

## Flow clusters and default views

Clusters are keyed by document, the author's own cut of the story into flows
([flow clusters](../docs/compiler/model/view.md#level-views)); the characters are read
off the members as the actors of the picture. Members in document order:
- `plot`: the scenes of plot.md whose statements carry `behavior` or `failure-mode`,
  every chapter in order. The four characters are its actors.
- `arcs`: the stance changes of arcs.md, when the transitions carry `behavior` (the
  usual judgment).
- `characters` and `readme`: the behavior their documents state, two or more members
  each.

Default views: `view:usecase/<doc-stem>` titled by the document, and
`view:sequence/<doc-stem>` over the members that carry an edge.
`view:state/ines-marlow`, `view:state/theo-brandt`. `view:object/scene`. One
`view:class/<scope>` per scope (one scope expected; its name is not graded).
`view:component/<root>` for each containment root with children (Port Alder, Marlow
family, Manuscript) derives mechanically and is not graded.

A statement narrating a scene is a `behavior` of the character who acts in it: a compile
whose plot statements all read `constraint` derives no plot flow and is a finding about
the extraction, not about the clustering.

## Planted traps

1. Cross-doc identity: plot.md calls Ines `Nessa` twice (ch3 "Dot tells Nessa", ch5
   "Callum asks Nessa"); characters.md explains the nickname. ONE entity
   `ent:ines-marlow` with `Nessa` in `aliases` and mentions in README.md,
   characters.md, settings.md, plot.md, and arcs.md; both Nessa scenes reference it. No
   `ent:nessa`. Secondary identity: The Lantern Room is defined in settings.md and used
   in every other document; one entity with mentions in at least 4 documents.
2. Contradiction: characters.md says Theo is 34; arcs.md says he is 36 when he arrives.
   Exactly one `contradiction` diagnostic with `ent:theo-brandt` among the subjects.
   Ines is 31 in both characters.md and arcs.md: no diagnostic.
3. Nondeterministic transition: arcs.md's Theo table sends acquaintance → rival on
   "Ines confronts Theo about the survey"; the midpoint paragraph sends acquaintance →
   ally on the same trigger. Both requirements exist with their transitions, and the
   state machine check files `nondeterministic-transition` on the pair. A session may
   also file `contradiction` on the pair; dropping either transition to silence the
   check is wrong (the fix belongs in the prose).
4. Non-normative hiding a rule: settings.md "Research notes" reads as outside-world
   background but contains "A written survey report takes three days to produce, so
   Theo's report cannot exist before chapter 3." Marking the section non-normative
   must trigger `suspicious-non-normative`; extracting the rule and marking the section
   covered is also correct.
5. Genuinely non-normative: style.md "Inspirations" states no obligation and is marked
   non-normative without a `suspicious-non-normative` finding. README.md "What is
   where" is navigation and may be marked the same way.
6. Junk bait: README.md lists the chapter files (`manuscript/01-arrival.md` ...) and
   the `manuscript/` directory. None of these become entities. Chapters as concepts
   (Chapter, or the eight numbered chapters under Manuscript) are legitimate.
7. Lookalike pairs that stay apart: `Marlow House` (a place), `the Marlow family` (a
   family), `Ines Marlow` (a person); and `the harbor ledger` (in the ferry office safe)
   versus `the takings ledger` (under the shop counter). settings.md says the two
   ledgers are never confused; merging any of these pairs is a failure.
8. Instance versus type: the worked scene in plot.md is an instance of Scene, not a
   refresh of Scene's attributes with values, and the 23 scene lines of the plot are
   requirements, never one entity per line.

## What the diagrams show

- Class (`view:class/<scope>`): the four characters with `age` and `occupation`, Scene
  with its four typed attributes, Chapter, Manuscript, the Marlow family, Port Alder,
  the Lantern Room, Marlow House, the harbor ledger, the harbor wall. Arrows:
  compositions Manuscript to Chapter to Scene, Marlow family to Ines, Port Alder to the
  Lantern Room and Marlow House; associations among the characters as stated. The
  notebook scene is absent (instances are excluded from the class query).
- Object (`view:object/scene`): one object `the notebook scene : Scene` with the four
  values.
- State (`view:state/ines-marlow`): `[*] --> stranger`, four arrows up to `beloved`.
  State (`view:state/theo-brandt`): `[*] --> stranger`, five arrows; two leave
  `acquaintance` with the same label, which is the visible nondeterminism.
- Use case (`view:usecase/plot`, `view:usecase/arcs`, and the other documents with two
  or more flow members): one use case per document, titled by the document; a character
  the members label `actor` connects to it as a stick figure.
- Sequence (`view:sequence/plot` and the others): messages between characters in
  chapter order, e.g. Ines → Dot "asks for the harbor ledger", Ines → Theo "confronts
  about the survey", Ines → Theo "asks Theo to stay".
- Activity: no default; a curated activity twin of the plot view shows the chapter 5
  failure as the branch (the lease page cut out, the council votes to proceed).
docs/README.md:
# The Lantern Room

This is the bible for *The Lantern Room*, a short romance novel set in the harbor town of
Port Alder. Everything the manuscript has to honor is written down here: who the
characters are, where the story happens, what happens in each chapter, how the two leads
change, and how the prose is written. The manuscript is the deliverable. This bible is
the source it is built from, and when the two disagree, the bible is what gets fixed
first.

## Premise

Port Alder's harbor wall is coming down. Pryce Maritime has bought the quay and plans to
replace the wall, and the row of shops standing on it, with a marina. Ines Marlow runs
the Lantern Room, a bookshop on that row that her family has kept for three generations.
Theo Brandt is the marine surveyor Pryce Maritime hires to survey the wall before the
demolition. He rents the room above the shop without saying who sent him.

The novel runs one autumn, from Theo's arrival on the ferry to the night of the storm
and the week after it. Ines and Theo fall in love over the fight for the wall; the
[arcs](./arcs.md) say how, one stance at a time. The wall stays up. The marina is never
built.

## The deliverable

The deliverable is the manuscript. The manuscript is a set of chapters, one markdown
file per chapter, in a directory called `manuscript/` beside this bible. The files are
numbered in reading order and named after the chapter title:

```
manuscript/01-arrival.md
manuscript/02-the-survey.md
manuscript/03-the-ledger.md
manuscript/04-the-quay.md
manuscript/05-the-council.md
manuscript/06-the-storm.md
manuscript/07-the-notebook.md
manuscript/08-the-lantern-room.md
```

The manuscript has eight chapters. Each chapter file begins with the chapter title as a
level-one heading and contains nothing but the chapter's prose after it: no notes, no
front matter, no scene labels.

Every chapter is a run of scenes. A scene has a point of view, a setting, a goal, and an
outcome. The point of view is the character whose head the scene stays in. The setting
is one of the places in [settings](./settings.md). The goal is what the point-of-view
character wants when the scene opens, and the outcome is what they have when it closes.
A scene never changes its point of view partway through. The [plot](./plot.md) lists
every scene and writes one of them out in full as a worked example.

## Continuity

Names are spelled one way in every chapter. Ines takes no accent. Port Alder is two
words. The Lantern Room is capitalized as a proper name, and the lantern in its window
is not. Theo's surname is Brandt with a t. Chapter titles in the manuscript match the
chapter titles in the plot.

## What is where

- [Characters](./characters.md): the four people in the book, who knows whom, and the
  Marlow family.
- [Settings](./settings.md): Port Alder and the places in it.
- [Plot](./plot.md): the chapters scene by scene, the plan that fails, and the worked
  scene.
- [Arcs](./arcs.md): how Ines and Theo move from stranger to beloved, and what moves
  them.
- [Style](./style.md): tense, point of view, chapter length, and the shelf of books this
  one grew out of.
docs/arcs.md:
# Arcs

Each lead moves through the same five stances toward the other: stranger, acquaintance,
rival, ally, beloved. Ines's stance is toward Theo and Theo's stance is toward Ines. A
stance changes only when something happens on the page, so every trigger below is a
scene in the [plot](./plot.md). Neither lead ever moves back down a stance.

Both leads start as strangers. Both end as beloved, and beloved is where the book leaves
them: nothing moves either lead out of it.

## Ines

Ines is 31 and has never had a reason to leave Port Alder. The arc gives her one, in the
shape of Theo's next contract, and she declines it. Her stance toward Theo changes four
times:

| From | To | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| stranger | acquaintance | Theo takes the upstairs room |
| acquaintance | rival | Dot tells Ines who Theo works for |
| rival | ally | Theo offers Ines the crack finding |
| ally | beloved | Theo shores up the wall through the storm |

The rival stretch is the long one, from chapter 3 to chapter 5, and it is where Ines is
wrong about Theo for reasons that are entirely his fault.

## Theo

Theo is 36 when he arrives and has been moving from job to job for twelve years. The arc
stops him. His stance toward Ines changes four times:

| From | To | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| stranger | acquaintance | Theo finds the crack beneath the Lantern Room |
| acquaintance | rival | Ines confronts Theo about the survey |
| rival | ally | Ines's plan fails at the council |
| ally | beloved | Ines asks Theo to stay |

Theo's first change happens before he has said ten words to Ines: finding the crack
under her shop makes her real to him before she is anything else.

## The midpoint

The midpoint is chapter 4, the confrontation on the quay. It is the scene the first half
points at and the second half looks back on, and it has to land both leads at once. When
Ines confronts Theo about the survey, Theo moves from acquaintance to ally. He has
already decided, on the wall at low tide, that she should know about the crack, and the
confrontation gives him the opening he was waiting for. Ines does not know this yet,
which is what makes chapter 5 hurt: she walks into the council believing him her enemy.

## Rules for the arcs

- A stance change is shown in a scene, never narrated in summary.
- Ines and Theo never change stance in the same scene.
- Each stance change is visible to the reader before the lead admits it to themselves.

# Characters

Four people carry the book. Ines and Theo carry the point of view; Callum and Dot are
seen only through them. Each character is introduced by age and occupation, then by what
they carry into the story.

## Ines Marlow

Ines Marlow. Age 31. Occupation: bookseller. She owns and runs the Lantern Room, the
bookshop on the quay, and has done since her mother died four years before the book
opens. She was born in Port Alder and has never lived anywhere else. Ines is a member of
the Marlow family, the last of it still living in the town.

Ines reads standing up. She keeps a pencil behind her ear and writes the day's takings
in the same ledger her grandmother used. She is quick to anger and slow to admit she was
wrong, and the book makes her do both.

Dot has called her Nessa since she was six, and Callum picked the name up at school.
Nobody else uses it, and Ines does not answer to it from strangers.

## Theo Brandt

Theo Brandt. Age 34. Occupation: marine surveyor. He works freelance for whoever is
paying, and this autumn Pryce Maritime is paying: Callum hires Theo to survey the harbor
wall before the demolition. Theo knows nobody in Port Alder when he arrives.

Theo keeps a field notebook and writes every measurement in it twice, once on site and
once again that evening. He does not lie, but he is comfortable not saying things. He
has moved eleven times in twelve years and owns nothing he cannot carry.

## Callum Pryce

Callum Pryce. Age 33. Occupation: project lead at Pryce Maritime, his father's company.
The marina is the first project with his name on it. Ines and Callum went to school
together and were close until they were nineteen.

Callum believes the marina will save the town, and the book lets him believe it. He is
not a villain and is not written as one, but he cuts the lease page out of the harbor
ledger, and he answers for it in chapter 7.

## Dot Feeney

Dot Feeney. Age 58. Occupation: ferry office manager. She runs the ferry office on the
quay and has done for thirty years. Dot has known Ines since Ines was six. Dot knows
everyone who steps off the ferry and everything that happens on the quay, and she keeps
the harbor ledger in the ferry office safe.

Dot is the first person in the book to know who Theo works for, and she tells Ines.

## The Marlow family

The Marlow family is Ines's family. The family has held the lease of the Lantern Room
for three generations, since Ines's grandmother signed it in 1961. The lease grants the
Marlows the quay frontage for as long as the harbor wall stands, which is why the lease
matters. Ines is the only Marlow who appears in the book; her grandmother and her mother
are spoken of but never seen.

## Who knows whom

- Ines and Callum know each other from school.
- Dot and Ines know each other; Dot is the nearest thing Ines has to family in the
  town.
- Callum and Theo know each other only through the contract: Callum hires Theo.
- Ines and Theo have never heard of each other before chapter 1.
- Dot and Theo meet when Theo steps off the ferry.

# Plot

Eight chapters, in reading order. Each scene below is one line naming who acts and what
they do; the manuscript expands every line into prose and adds nothing that changes what
happens. Scenes inside a chapter run in the order listed. The chapter titles are the
file names of the [deliverable](./README.md#the-deliverable) without the number.

## Chapter 1: Arrival

- Theo arrives in Port Alder on the afternoon ferry with one bag and a case of survey
  instruments.
- Dot meets Theo at the ferry office and sends him along the quay to the Lantern Room
  for a room.
- Ines lets the upstairs room to Theo without asking what brings him to town.

## Chapter 2: The survey

- Theo walks the harbor wall at low tide and finds a crack in the footing directly
  beneath the Lantern Room.
- Callum tells Theo to leave the crack out of the written report, because a wall that
  can be repaired is a wall the council will not demolish.

## Chapter 3: The ledger

- Dot tells Nessa who Theo works for.
- Ines asks Dot for the harbor ledger, the book in the ferry office safe that records
  every lease on the quay.
- Ines finds the Marlow lease in the harbor ledger and reads the clause that grants the
  frontage for as long as the wall stands.
- Ines decides to take the lease to the harbor council and block the demolition.

## Chapter 4: The quay

- Ines confronts Theo on the quay about the survey and asks him what he found.
- Theo refuses to show Ines the report and tells her to ask Callum.

## Chapter 5: The council

- Callum asks Nessa to drop the petition, for old times' sake.
- Ines presents the harbor ledger to the harbor council to block the demolition.
- The plan fails: when Ines opens the ledger at the meeting, the lease page has been cut
  out, and the council votes to proceed with the demolition.
- Theo offers Ines the crack finding as proof that the wall can be repaired instead of
  replaced.

## Chapter 6: The storm

- Dot closes the ferry office when the storm warning comes and turns the last ferry
  back.
- Theo shores up the crack with the harbor crew through the night of the storm.
- Ines keeps the lantern lit and the kettle on for the crew until dawn.

## Chapter 7: The notebook

- Ines finds Theo's field notebook in the upstairs room and reads the measurements he
  wrote down twice.
- Ines gives the notebook to the harbor council as evidence that the crack was known
  and left out of the report.
- Callum admits to the council that he cut the lease page out of the ledger and
  withdraws the marina plan.

## Chapter 8: The Lantern Room

- Theo turns down the next contract and stays in Port Alder.
- Ines asks Theo to stay, and he tells her he already has.

## A worked scene

One scene written out the way the [deliverable](./README.md#the-deliverable) defines a
scene, to check that the definition holds. The notebook scene is the first scene of
chapter 7:

- Point of view: Ines.
- Setting: the upstairs room of the Lantern Room.
- Goal: Ines wants to put Theo's notebook back in his bag before he notices it is out.
- Outcome: she keeps it, reads it, and takes it to the council.

Every scene in the manuscript can be written out this way. This one is the check that
the template holds, and chapter 7 of the manuscript opens with it.

# Settings

The whole book happens in Port Alder. Three places matter; everything else is a street
the characters walk along between them.

## Port Alder

Port Alder is a harbor town on the west coast with about four thousand residents. The
town climbs a hill above a stone harbor wall, and the quay runs along the top of the
wall. The ferry is the only way in that does not mean a two-hour drive around the
estuary. In autumn the ferry crosses four times a day, and it does not run after dark.

The harbor wall was built in 1840 and was last surveyed in 1988. The quay carries a row
of six shops, and the Lantern Room is the third from the ferry office. The harbor
council owns the wall and leases the quay frontage to the shops standing on it.

## The Lantern Room

The Lantern Room is a bookshop on the quay in Port Alder. It has two floors: the shop on
the ground floor and a single room above it, which Ines lets to lodgers when she needs
the money. The shop is named for the ship's lantern that hangs in the front window, and
the lantern is lit every evening at dusk.

The shop opens at nine and closes at six, and it does not open on Sundays. The takings
ledger lives under the counter, where Ines writes the day's takings in pencil. The
harbor ledger does not live in the shop: it lives in the ferry office safe, and the two
ledgers are never confused on the page.

The upstairs room has one window, facing the harbor, and the crack Theo finds runs
directly beneath it.

## Marlow House

Marlow House is the Marlow family's house on Chapel Lane in Port Alder, up the hill from
the harbor. Ines lives there alone. The house has been in the family as long as the shop
lease, and the two are spoken of together. No scene of the novel is set inside Marlow
House: it is seen from the quay and mentioned, never entered.

## Research notes

Things I looked up while outlining, kept here so I do not look them up twice. A harbor
wall survey has three parts, a walkover, core samples, and a written report. Surveyors
write the report from the field notebook rather than from memory, which is why the
notebook carries the plot. A written survey report takes three days to produce, so
Theo's report cannot exist before chapter 3. West coast ferries publish their autumn
timetables in late August. A stone bookshop in October holds a temperature of about
twelve degrees.
docs/style.md:
# Style

How the prose is written. These are rules for the manuscript, not suggestions; a chapter
that breaks one is not finished.

## Tense and point of view

The manuscript is written in the past tense. The point of view is close third person:
the narration stays inside one character's head per scene and reports only what that
character sees, hears, and thinks. The narrator never comments from outside the scene.

Point of view alternates between Ines and Theo chapter by chapter. Odd chapters belong
to Ines and even chapters belong to Theo, so chapter 1 opens in Ines's head watching the
ferry come in and chapter 8 closes in Theo's. Within a chapter every scene keeps the
chapter's point of view; a scene that needs the other lead's head goes in the other
lead's chapter.

Callum and Dot never carry the point of view. What they think is shown only through what
Ines or Theo sees them do.

## Length

Each chapter runs between 2,000 and 3,500 words. The whole manuscript runs under 24,000
words. A chapter that comes in short is padded with nothing: it is cut from the outline
instead, and the plot page is changed to match.

## Prose rules

- Dialogue uses double quotation marks and a new paragraph per speaker.
- No scene opens on the weather, except the first scene of chapter 6, which opens on
  the storm warning.
- The word "love" is not said aloud by either lead before chapter 8.
- Theo's measurements are given in metres and centimetres, never feet, because that is
  how he writes them in the notebook.
- Ines never calls the shop "the bookshop"; to her it is the shop or the Lantern Room.
- Nobody explains the lease clause in dialogue; the reader gets it when Ines reads it,
  in chapter 3, from the page.

## Inspirations

None of this is a rule, and nothing in the manuscript is checked against it. These are
the books and films I reread while outlining, listed so I remember where I was standing
when I started, not so anyone matches them:

- *Persuasion*, Jane Austen.
- *The Shipping News*, Annie Proulx.
- *Local Hero*, the 1983 film.
- *84, Charing Cross Road*, Helene Hanff.
- *The Lighthouse Stevensons*, Bella Bathurst.

    raw: |
      # The Lantern Room

      This is the bible for *The Lantern Room*, a short romance novel set in the harbor town of
      Port Alder. Everything the manuscript has to honor is written down here: who the
      characters are, where the story happens, what happens in each chapter, how the two leads
      change, and how the prose is written. The manuscript is the deliverable. This bible is
      the source it is built from, and when the two disagree, the bible is what gets fixed
      first.
    hash: dcaf42c3665bdda1

  /the-lantern-room/continuity:
    title: Continuity
    kind: heading
    order: 2
    parent: /the-lantern-room
    raw: |
      ## Continuity

      Names are spelled one way in every chapter. Ines takes no accent. Port Alder is two
      words. The Lantern Room is capitalized as a proper name, and the lantern in its window
      is not. Theo's surname is Brandt with a t. Chapter titles in the manuscript match the
      chapter titles in the plot.
    hash: 7814cfc2ad7cb380
    lines:
    - 50
    - 57
  /the-lantern-room/premise:
    title: Premise
    kind: heading
    order: 0
    parent: /the-lantern-room
    raw: |
      ## Premise

      Port Alder's harbor wall is coming down. Pryce Maritime has bought the quay and plans to
      replace the wall, and the row of shops standing on it, with a marina. Ines Marlow runs
      the Lantern Room, a bookshop on that row that her family has kept for three generations.
      Theo Brandt is the marine surveyor Pryce Maritime hires to survey the wall before the
      demolition. He rents the room above the shop without saying who sent him.

      The novel runs one autumn, from Theo's arrival on the ferry to the night of the storm
      and the week after it. Ines and Theo fall in love over the fight for the wall; the
      [arcs](./arcs.md) say how, one stance at a time. The wall stays up. The marina is never
      built.
    hash: cc8ec89c277a5c5d
    lines:
    - 9

  /the-lantern-room/the-deliverable:
    title: The deliverable
    kind: heading
    order: 1
    parent: /the-lantern-room
    raw: |
      ## The deliverable

      The deliverable is the manuscript. The manuscript is a set of chapters, one markdown
      file per chapter, in a directory called `manuscript/` beside this bible. The files are
      numbered in reading order and named after the chapter title:

      ```
      manuscript/01-arrival.md
      manuscript/02-the-survey.md
      manuscript/03-the-ledger.md
      manuscript/04-the-quay.md
      manuscript/05-the-council.md
      manuscript/06-the-storm.md
      manuscript/07-the-notebook.md
      manuscript/08-the-lantern-room.md
      ```

      The manuscript has eight chapters. Each chapter file begins with the chapter title as a
      level-one heading and contains nothing but the chapter's prose after it: no notes, no
      front matter, no scene labels.

      Every chapter is a run of scenes. A scene has a point of view, a setting, a goal, and an
      outcome. The point of view is the character whose head the scene stays in. The setting
      is one of the places in [settings](./settings.md). The goal is what the point-of-view
      character wants when the scene opens, and the outcome is what they have when it closes.
      A scene never changes its point of view partway through. The [plot](./plot.md) lists
      every scene and writes one of them out in full as a worked example.

sections:
  /arcs:
    title: Arcs
    kind: root
    order: 0
    raw: |
      # Arcs

      Each lead moves through the same five stances toward the other: stranger, acquaintance,
      rival, ally, beloved. Ines's stance is toward Theo and Theo's stance is toward Ines. A
      stance changes only when something happens on the page, so every trigger below is a
      scene in the [plot](./plot.md). Neither lead ever moves back down a stance.

      Both leads start as strangers. Both end as beloved, and beloved is where the book leaves
      them: nothing moves either lead out of it.
    hash: 4e9343fd70243df8
    lines:
    - 0
    - 10
  /arcs/ines:
    title: Ines
    kind: heading
    order: 0
    parent: /arcs
    raw: |
      ## Ines

      Ines is 31 and has never had a reason to leave Port Alder. The arc gives her one, in the
      shape of Theo's next contract, and she declines it. Her stance toward Theo changes four
      times:

      | From | To | Trigger |
      | --- | --- | --- |
      | stranger | acquaintance | Theo takes the upstairs room |
      | acquaintance | rival | Dot tells Ines who Theo works for |
      | rival | ally | Theo offers Ines the crack finding |
      | ally | beloved | Theo shores up the wall through the storm |

      The rival stretch is the long one, from chapter 3 to chapter 5, and it is where Ines is
      wrong about Theo for reasons that are entirely his fault.
    hash: 4fac50768b3f9da0
    lines:
    - 10
    - 26
  /arcs/rules-for-the-arcs:
    title: Rules for the arcs
    kind: heading
    order: 3
    parent: /arcs
    raw: |-
      ## Rules for the arcs

      - A stance change is shown in a scene, never narrated in summary.
      - Ines and Theo never change stance in the same scene.
      - Each stance change is visible to the reader before the lead admits it to themselves.
    hash: 7b6812617fe3bc12
    lines:
    - 50
    - 55
  /arcs/the-midpoint:
    title: The midpoint
    kind: heading
    order: 2
    parent: /arcs
    raw: |
      ## The midpoint

      The midpoint is chapter 4, the confrontation on the quay. It is the scene the first half
      points at and the second half looks back on, and it has to land both leads at once. When
      Ines confronts Theo about the survey, Theo moves from acquaintance to ally. He has
      already decided, on the wall at low tide, that she should know about the crack, and the
      confrontation gives him the opening he was waiting for. Ines does not know this yet,
      which is what makes chapter 5 hurt: she walks into the council believing him her enemy.
    hash: 5dde2898c8781654
    lines:
    - 41
    - 50
  /arcs/theo:
    title: Theo
    kind: heading
    order: 1
    parent: /arcs
    raw: |
      ## Theo

      Theo is 36 when he arrives and has been moving from job to job for twelve years. The arc
      stops him. His stance toward Ines changes four times:

      | From | To | Trigger |
      | --- | --- | --- |
      | stranger | acquaintance | Theo finds the crack beneath the Lantern Room |
      | acquaintance | rival | Ines confronts Theo about the survey |
      | rival | ally | Ines's plan fails at the council |
      | ally | beloved | Ines asks Theo to stay |

      Theo's first change happens before he has said ten words to Ines: finding the crack
      under her shop makes her real to him before she is anything else.
    hash: 4eeac0132e341362

    - 26
    - 41

      # Characters

      Four people carry the book. Ines and Theo carry the point of view; Callum and Dot are
      seen only through them. Each character is introduced by age and occupation, then by what
      they carry into the story.
    hash: 71802bdede9e564f

  /characters/callum-pryce:
    title: Callum Pryce
    kind: heading
    order: 2
    parent: /characters
    raw: |
      ## Callum Pryce

      Callum Pryce. Age 33. Occupation: project lead at Pryce Maritime, his father's company.
      The marina is the first project with his name on it. Ines and Callum went to school
      together and were close until they were nineteen.

      Callum believes the marina will save the town, and the book lets him believe it. He is
      not a villain and is not written as one, but he cuts the lease page out of the harbor
      ledger, and he answers for it in chapter 7.
    hash: 9f881243c962aacd
    lines:
    - 30
    - 40
  /characters/dot-feeney:
    title: Dot Feeney
    kind: heading
    order: 3
    parent: /characters
    raw: |
      ## Dot Feeney

      Dot Feeney. Age 58. Occupation: ferry office manager. She runs the ferry office on the
      quay and has done for thirty years. Dot has known Ines since Ines was six. Dot knows
      everyone who steps off the ferry and everything that happens on the quay, and she keeps
      the harbor ledger in the ferry office safe.

      Dot is the first person in the book to know who Theo works for, and she tells Ines.
    hash: db5f364b0e70d97c
    lines:
    - 40
    - 49
  /characters/ines-marlow:
    title: Ines Marlow
    kind: heading
    order: 0
    parent: /characters
    raw: |
      ## Ines Marlow

      Ines Marlow. Age 31. Occupation: bookseller. She owns and runs the Lantern Room, the
      bookshop on the quay, and has done since her mother died four years before the book
      opens. She was born in Port Alder and has never lived anywhere else. Ines is a member of
      the Marlow family, the last of it still living in the town.

      Ines reads standing up. She keeps a pencil behind her ear and writes the day's takings
      in the same ledger her grandmother used. She is quick to anger and slow to admit she was
      wrong, and the book makes her do both.

      Dot has called her Nessa since she was six, and Callum picked the name up at school.
      Nobody else uses it, and Ines does not answer to it from strangers.
    hash: d9f1d32703dd2714
    lines:
    - 6
    - 20
  /characters/the-marlow-family:
    title: The Marlow family
    kind: heading
    order: 4
    parent: /characters
    raw: |
      ## The Marlow family

      The Marlow family is Ines's family. The family has held the lease of the Lantern Room
      for three generations, since Ines's grandmother signed it in 1961. The lease grants the
      Marlows the quay frontage for as long as the harbor wall stands, which is why the lease
      matters. Ines is the only Marlow who appears in the book; her grandmother and her mother
      are spoken of but never seen.
    hash: 21f9882695c69790
    lines:
    - 49
    - 57
  /characters/theo-brandt:
    title: Theo Brandt
    kind: heading
    order: 1
    parent: /characters
    raw: |
      ## Theo Brandt

      Theo Brandt. Age 34. Occupation: marine surveyor. He works freelance for whoever is
      paying, and this autumn Pryce Maritime is paying: Callum hires Theo to survey the harbor
      wall before the demolition. Theo knows nobody in Port Alder when he arrives.

      Theo keeps a field notebook and writes every measurement in it twice, once on site and
      once again that evening. He does not lie, but he is comfortable not saying things. He
      has moved eleven times in twelve years and owns nothing he cannot carry.
    hash: c15744a9ebb99564
    lines:
    - 20
    - 30
  /characters/who-knows-whom:
    title: Who knows whom
    kind: heading
    order: 5
    parent: /characters
    raw: |-
      ## Who knows whom

      - Ines and Callum know each other from school.
      - Dot and Ines know each other; Dot is the nearest thing Ines has to family in the
        town.
      - Callum and Theo know each other only through the contract: Callum hires Theo.
      - Ines and Theo have never heard of each other before chapter 1.
      - Dot and Theo meet when Theo steps off the ferry.
    hash: b9c293333d888bb1

      One scene written out the way the [deliverable](./README.md#the-deliverable) defines a

      # Settings

      The whole book happens in Port Alder. Three places matter; everything else is a street
      the characters walk along between them.
    hash: 2a5bfa5ad740aaab

  /settings/marlow-house:
    title: Marlow House
    kind: heading
    order: 2
    parent: /settings
    raw: |
      ## Marlow House

      Marlow House is the Marlow family's house on Chapel Lane in Port Alder, up the hill from
      the harbor. Ines lives there alone. The house has been in the family as long as the shop
      lease, and the two are spoken of together. No scene of the novel is set inside Marlow
      House: it is seen from the quay and mentioned, never entered.
    hash: e22d9c4edfd65020

    - 31

  /settings/port-alder:
    title: Port Alder
    kind: heading
    order: 0
    parent: /settings
    raw: |
      ## Port Alder

      Port Alder is a harbor town on the west coast with about four thousand residents. The
      town climbs a hill above a stone harbor wall, and the quay runs along the top of the
      wall. The ferry is the only way in that does not mean a two-hour drive around the
      estuary. In autumn the ferry crosses four times a day, and it does not run after dark.

      The harbor wall was built in 1840 and was last surveyed in 1988. The quay carries a row
      of six shops, and the Lantern Room is the third from the ferry office. The harbor
      council owns the wall and leases the quay frontage to the shops standing on it.
    hash: 8dfd0ff4831407f6
    lines:
    - 5
    - 16
  /settings/research-notes:
    title: Research notes
    kind: heading
    order: 3
    parent: /settings
    raw: |-
      ## Research notes

      Things I looked up while outlining, kept here so I do not look them up twice. A harbor
      wall survey has three parts, a walkover, core samples, and a written report. Surveyors
      write the report from the field notebook rather than from memory, which is why the
      notebook carries the plot. A written survey report takes three days to produce, so
      Theo's report cannot exist before chapter 3. West coast ferries publish their autumn
      timetables in late August. A stone bookshop in October holds a temperature of about
      twelve degrees.
    hash: dc33277aa3e0a242
    lines:
    - 38
    - 47
  /settings/the-lantern-room:
    title: The Lantern Room
    kind: heading
    order: 1
    parent: /settings
    raw: |
      ## The Lantern Room

      The Lantern Room is a bookshop on the quay in Port Alder. It has two floors: the shop on
      the ground floor and a single room above it, which Ines lets to lodgers when she needs
      the money. The shop is named for the ship's lantern that hangs in the front window, and
      the lantern is lit every evening at dusk.

      The shop opens at nine and closes at six, and it does not open on Sundays. The takings
      ledger lives under the counter, where Ines writes the day's takings in pencil. The
      harbor ledger does not live in the shop: it lives in the ferry office safe, and the two
      ledgers are never confused on the page.

      The upstairs room has one window, facing the harbor, and the crack Theo finds runs
      directly beneath it.
    hash: 546c17502e9990bd

sections:

    title: Style
    kind: root

      # Style

      How the prose is written. These are rules for the manuscript, not suggestions; a chapter
      that breaks one is not finished.

  /style/inspirations:
    title: Inspirations
    kind: heading
    order: 3
    parent: /style
    raw: |-
      ## Inspirations

      None of this is a rule, and nothing in the manuscript is checked against it. These are
      the books and films I reread while outlining, listed so I remember where I was standing
      when I started, not so anyone matches them:

      - *Persuasion*, Jane Austen.
      - *The Shipping News*, Annie Proulx.
      - *Local Hero*, the 1983 film.
      - *84, Charing Cross Road*, Helene Hanff.
      - *The Lighthouse Stevensons*, Bella Bathurst.
    hash: 36844211c0862a9d
    lines:
    - 38
    - 49
  /style/length:
    title: Length
    kind: heading
    order: 1
    parent: /style
    raw: |
      ## Length

      Each chapter runs between 2,000 and 3,500 words. The whole manuscript runs under 24,000
      words. A chapter that comes in short is padded with nothing: it is cut from the outline
      instead, and the plot page is changed to match.
    hash: dbdfe66010188bf2
    lines:
    - 20
    - 26
  /style/prose-rules:
    title: Prose rules
    kind: heading
    order: 2
    parent: /style
    raw: |
      ## Prose rules

      - Dialogue uses double quotation marks and a new paragraph per speaker.
      - No scene opens on the weather, except the first scene of chapter 6, which opens on
        the storm warning.
      - The word "love" is not said aloud by either lead before chapter 8.
      - Theo's measurements are given in metres and centimetres, never feet, because that is
        how he writes them in the notebook.
      - Ines never calls the shop "the bookshop"; to her it is the shop or the Lantern Room.
      - Nobody explains the lease clause in dialogue; the reader gets it when Ines reads it,
        in chapter 3, from the page.
    hash: 402bc94d369a169c
    lines:
    - 26
    - 38
  /style/tense-and-point-of-view:
    title: Tense and point of view
    kind: heading
    order: 0
    parent: /style
    raw: |
      ## Tense and point of view

      The manuscript is written in the past tense. The point of view is close third person:
      the narration stays inside one character's head per scene and reports only what that
      character sees, hears, and thinks. The narrator never comments from outside the scene.

      Point of view alternates between Ines and Theo chapter by chapter. Odd chapters belong
      to Ines and even chapters belong to Theo, so chapter 1 opens in Ines's head watching the
      ferry come in and chapter 8 closes in Theo's. Within a chapter every scene keeps the
      chapter's point of view; a scene that needs the other lead's head goes in the other
      lead's chapter.

      Callum and Dot never carry the point of view. What they think is shown only through what
      Ines or Theo sees them do.
    hash: e395417a98afb39e
    lines:
    - 5
    - 20
